title: How To Get Your Students To Feel Remorse For Misbehavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that genuine student remorse comes not from teacher lectures or guilt trips but from shifting responsibility for behavior squarely onto students themselves. He lays out five practices to make this shift: defining rules precisely so there is no gray area, ensuring students understand their larger purpose in being at school, being explicit that the teacher's job is to teach rather than manage compliance, showing students how rules protect their own right to learn, and following through consistently on consequences. He warns that inconsistency undermines the entire system by signaling that rules don't really matter. When done well, he argues, even a simple warning can trigger authentic self-reflection and empathy rather than resentment.
points: Argues that authentic student remorse requires shifting responsibility for behavior onto students rather than lecturing or guilting them.
Recommends defining classroom rules with total precision so that breaking them is unmistakably a student's own choice.
Insists teachers should model that their job is to deliver world-class lessons, not to beg, threaten, or manage misbehavior.
Frames consistent follow-through as essential; inconsistency signals to students that the rules don't actually matter.
Contends that avoiding friction with students preserves rapport and reinforces that consequences—not the teacher's emotions—are driving accountability.
quotes: There must be no doubt among your students what does and doesn’t constitute breaking each rule. Thus, you must define your boundaries precisely.
Your job isn’t to accept shoddy performance, do their work for them, or let them off the hook. It isn’t to threaten, beg, or implore them to behave or give effort.
If you aren’t consistent, then you’re communicating to your students that none of the above is true. You’re telling them very clearly that your rules don’t even matter enough for you to follow them.
Shifting responsibility for listening, learning, and behaving over to your students reframes misbehavior entirely. It makes it seem immature, absurd, even embarrassing.
It isn’t thrust upon them as a guilt trip, which then is summarily rejected. It isn’t an outside force they can ignore, deny, or refuse to acknowledge.
No, it comes from inside the student. Where real change happens.
